prompt.context: Regional Jet Corporation is a U.S. manufacturer of regional airplanes—airplanes with 100 seats or less. Its business consists of two types of aircraft: (1) jet engine, 80 to 100-seat aircraft and (2) propeller, 20 to 30-seat aircraft. In fiscal year 1999, Regional Jet delivered 100 jet engine aircraft and 150 props. This represented a unit volume increase year-over-year of 10% and 5%, respectively, and revenues of $730 million and $225 million, respectively. Although overall profitability for Regional Jet in 1999 was a competitive 5% economic profit margin, profitability varied significantly by business. The prop business generated a stellar 30% profit margin, while the jet engine business was unprofitable with a margin of -3%. Over the past several years, Regional Jet has experienced eroding profitability in its jet engine aircraft business. Its prop business, despite being profitable, has been flat in most recent years. At a January 5th analyst conference, Regional Jet's senior management team announced that the company was committed to managing for value. To this end, Regional Jet has hired you and a team of consultants to help the company develop and implement value-maximizing strategies for its businesses.
prompt.question: For our case discussion today, please focus on the jet engine aircraft business: (1) How would you go about further analyzing this business? (2) What recommendations would you like to make to senior management?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the jet engine regional aircraft market?
clarifying_info.a: In 1999, the U.S. jet engine, 100-seat-or-less aircraft market was approximately $5 billion.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors and what are their market shares?
clarifying_info.a: There is no dominant competitor. The market leader has 20% market share. There are 4 other competitors with market share from 12% to 18%. Regional Jet Corporation has approximately 16% share.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is the market growing?
clarifying_info.a: The market has been growing approximately 5% in units delivered each year for the past 5 years and is expected to continue growing 5% over the next decade. In 1999, a total of 625 jet engine regional aircraft were delivered to customers.
The supplier base for regional aircraft parts is highly fragmented and Regional Jet uses approximately 50% proprietary parts in its jet engine aircraft. Supplier power is low.

In 1999, there were 225 customers. Types include airlines, aircraft lessors, local and national governments, businesses, and private individuals. Customer power varies by segment. Aircraft lessors make large purchases (often 20 or more aircraft) in a buying cycle and exploit their negotiating leverage. All other customers have low-to-moderate buying power.

clarifying_info.q: What is Regional Jet's offering position relative to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Overall, parity. The cockpit is similar to the industry standard (low switching costs). Range is 500 miles, similar to market average. Maintenance costs over asset life are in line with competitors. Average aircraft life is 20 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the threat from larger jets?
clarifying_info.a: Larger commercial jets (100 seats or greater) can be used on regional routes but are expensive to operate solely on a regional basis. Intensity of indirect competition is low.

Jet engine regional aircraft manufacturing requires significant capital investment in production facilities and equipment, as well as strong relationships with various labor unions. Barriers to entry are high.

framework: I. Market Economics — assess market size, growth, profitability, and structural forces (Porter's Five Forces: supplier power, customer power, competitive intensity, indirect competition, barriers to entry)
II. Competitive Position — assess Regional Jet's offering position, pricing position, and operating position relative to competitors
III. Customer Segmentation — identify customer segments, analyze profitability by segment, and identify the key driver of profitability differences
IV. Overall Competitive Position — synthesize findings to judge whether Regional Jet is advantaged, at parity, or disadvantaged overall
V. Strategy Alternatives — generate and evaluate strategic options to improve jet engine aircraft profitability

questions.prompt: What is the overall market profitability and structural assessment of the jet engine regional aircraft industry?
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply a Five Forces framework. Supplier power is LOW (fragmented base, 50% proprietary parts). Direct competition intensity is LOW-TO-MODERATE (only 6 manufacturers, fairly concentrated). Customer power VARIES — aircraft lessors have HIGH power due to large volume purchases; other customers have low-to-moderate power. Indirect competition is LOW (larger jets too expensive to operate regionally). Barriers to entry are HIGH (capital-intensive, labor union relationships). Conclusion: the market is profitable. Average competitor generates 4% economic profit margins over the past 5 years.

questions.prompt: What is Regional Jet's offering, pricing, and operating position relative to competitors?
questions.guidance: Offering: PARITY — standard cockpit (low switching cost), 500-mile range (market average), maintenance cost in line with competitors. Operating: PARITY — operating cost per aircraft is at parity with the industry; every jet delivered cost approximately the same to produce. Pricing: DISADVANTAGED — Regional Jet is gaining market share (10% unit growth vs. 5% market growth) with a parity offering, which implies it is pricing below market average (pricing for share).

questions.prompt: Calculate the average price per aircraft by customer segment. What does this reveal?
questions.guidance: Since operating cost per aircraft is the same for all segments, differences in profitability are driven entirely by price. A strong candidate computes average revenue per aircraft by segment without prompting.

math.setup: Average price = Segment revenues / Segment aircraft delivered. Use Exhibit 2 Profitability by Customer Segment data.
steps: Difference: lessors pay $1.2mm–$1.6mm less per aircraft than other segments
math.answer: Lessors pay ~$6.8mm per aircraft vs. $8.4mm (buy-1) and $8.0mm (buy-3). The sole driver of lessor segment unprofitability is price — lessors exploit buying power to extract large concessions. Total economic cost per aircraft is $7.858mm, meaning lessors are sold below total economic cost.

questions.prompt: What is Regional Jet's overall competitive position?
questions.guidance: DISADVANTAGED overall. The market is profitable (avg. 4% economic profit) but Regional Jet earns -3% economic profit margin. This is driven by a disadvantaged pricing position, particularly to the large lessor customer segment which accounts for 60% of aircraft delivered and generates -$33mm economic profit. Offering and operating positions are at parity, so pricing is the sole differentiator.

questions.prompt: How long would it take to double the jet engine business's economic profit if Regional Jet pursues only new small and medium (non-lessor) customers at the market growth rate of 5%?
questions.guidance: Current economic profit from non-lessor segments: $3mm (buy-1) + $11mm (buy-3) = $14mm. Current total economic profit is -$20mm; doubling that target is not straightforward — interpret as doubling the value of the business from its current state, or growing to a positive and doubled profit level. The key insight is that this path is a slow road to profitability given only 5% annual growth, and is unlikely to result in a dramatic near-term improvement. Candidate should flag slow growth and scale risk.

math.setup: Current non-lessor economic profit = $3mm + $11mm = $14mm. At 5% growth per year, years to double this contribution (to $28mm from non-lessor) while the lessor drag remains.
steps: At 5% annual growth: Year 1 = $14.7mm, Year 5 ≈ $17.9mm, Year 10 ≈ $22.8mm, Year 15 ≈ $29.1mm
Approximate 15 years to double non-lessor EP to $28mm without changing lessor economics
math.answer: Roughly 14–15 years to double non-lessor economic profit at 5% market growth — a slow road to value creation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are strategy alternatives that Regional Jet can pursue to improve jet engine aircraft profitability?

categories.name: Alternative 1: Pursue non-lessor customers only (no increase to lessors)
ideas: Aggressively target small and medium customers (buy-1 and buy-3 segments) where pricing is above total economic cost
Gradually reduce lessor dependence while growing profitable segments
Key risk: slow path — only 5% market growth rate; roughly 14–15 years to meaningfully improve profitability
Does not address existing lessor book or leverage scale

categories.name: Alternative 2: Exit lessors entirely
ideas: Stop serving aircraft lessors altogether and redirect all capacity to small/medium customers

Key risk: lessors currently account for 60% of units delivered (60 of 100); losing them destroys scale and spreads fixed costs over far fewer units, potentially making even profitable segments unprofitable
Current per-unit economics assume 100 units of output; at 40 units fixed costs per unit would rise sharply

categories.name: Alternative 3: Enter the aircraft leasing market
ideas: Regional Jet enters the leasing market directly, competing with its own lessor customers
Increases negotiating leverage vis-a-vis lessors
Aircraft leasing market is large: nearly 50% of new aircraft delivered in 1999 are leased (operating leases half of that); growing 5%/year
Market is profitable: average competitor ROE ~15% vs. cost of equity ~10%
Three lessors dominate with 65% combined share
Key driver of leasing profitability: cost of funds — Regional Jet would be at parity
Regional Jet already has marketing relationships with end-users (airlines, govts, businesses) who lease from current lessor customers
Regional Jet already provides limited vendor/manufacturer financing
Key questions: capital requirements, regulatory considerations, impact on lessor customer relationships, ability to build leasing expertise

categories.name: Other alternatives
ideas: Negotiate better pricing terms with lessors through volume discounts structured differently
Improve operating efficiency to lower the $7,858k total economic cost per aircraft
Exit jet engine business and focus on the profitable prop business
Pursue a joint venture or partnership with a leasing company

recommendation: Regional Jet is competitively disadvantaged in the jet engine aircraft business, earning -3% economic profit margin in a market that generates +4% on average. The root cause is a pricing disadvantage driven almost entirely by the lessor customer segment, which uses its high buying power to extract price concessions of ~$1–1.6mm per aircraft below what other customers pay — and below the total economic cost of $7.858mm per unit.

The recommended strategy is to pursue Alternative 3: enter the aircraft leasing market. This directly addresses the root cause (lessor buying power) by making Regional Jet a competitor rather than a captive supplier. It leverages existing end-user relationships and limited vendor-financing capabilities, and enters an attractive and growing market with positive economics (ROE 15% vs. 10% cost of equity).
As a complementary measure, Regional Jet should also aggressively pursue profitable small and medium (non-lessor) customers to improve mix and reduce dependence on lessors over time.
risks: Entering leasing requires significant capital investment and funding capacity
Lessor customers may retaliate by purchasing from competitors, accelerating loss of scale
Regional Jet lacks leasing expertise; operational execution risk is high
Cost of funds parity assumption may not hold if credit rating is affected by increased leverage
Regulatory and accounting complexity of holding a leasing portfolio
next_steps: Conduct a detailed feasibility and financial model for an aircraft leasing subsidiary
Assess capital structure implications and funding sources (debt, equity, securitization)
Evaluate partnership or acquisition of a smaller leasing platform to accelerate entry
Map out current end-user relationships to quantify addressable leasing pipeline
Define a negotiating strategy toward existing lessor customers during transition period
